headline: Nobel Peace Prize honors Navi Pillay's lifelong fight for justice
meta_description: Former UN human rights chief Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize for her decades of work prosecuting war crimes and defending human rights across the globe.
summary_short: Navi Pillay, who defended Nelson Mandela during apartheid and served as UN human rights chief, has been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her work promoting internationa…
body:
Navi Pillay, the former UN human rights chief, has been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her exceptional efforts to advance peace and international law. The Norwegian Nobel Committee recognized her "exceptional courage and integrity" in leading the world toward a more comprehensive global legal order, particularly her instrumental role in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted. Over a career spanning more than fifty years—from fighting apartheid in South Africa to defending civilians in conflict zones—Pillay has become a steadfast voice for justice on the world stage.

Pillay's journey traces a remarkable arc through some of history's most consequential moments. Born in South Africa in 1941 to a Tamil Indian family, she became the first non-white woman to establish a legal practice in her country. As a defence attorney, she exposed torture and helped secure rights for prisoners on Robben Island, then served as a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, where she established groundbreaking legal precedents in prosecuting genocide and gender-based violence. She later chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and held the post of UN human rights chief from 2008 to 2014.

What makes Pillay's recognition particularly poignant is the timing. In an October 2025 interview, she reflected on how the end of apartheid—which she never expected to witness—came through the collective support of people worldwide. That belief in international solidarity has shaped her entire career. Current UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the award "a reaffirmation that human rights, the rule of law, justice and accountability are fundamental to everything—to peace, to security and prosperity." The prize stands as recognition not just of one woman's courage, but of everyone dedicated to defending human rights, often at great personal risk.
quick_facts: Former UN human rights chief awarded Nobel Peace Prize for 50+ years of justice work
First non-white woman to establish a legal practice in South Africa
Served as judge at International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and International Criminal Court
Defended anti-apartheid activists including Nelson Mandela's supporters on Robben Island
